name: Majumdar-Papapetrou Extremal Black Holes
description: Any number of extremal charged black holes at rest, the static electrovacuum solution Sudhansu Datta Majumdar and Achilles Papapetrou found independently in 1947. Between every pair of holes the electric repulsion balances the gravitational attraction exactly, so the holes stay at rest in any arrangement.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. Each hole carries the mass parameter $m_i = GM_i/c^2$, a length, and a charge $Q_i$ of one common sign with $GQ_i^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4) = m_i^2$.
history: In the static, axially symmetric electrovacuum fields Hermann Weyl found in 1917, the surfaces of constant gravitational and electric potential coincide, so the field equations become linear and solutions can be superposed [weyl1917, griffiths2009]. Sudhansu Datta Majumdar dropped the symmetry in 1947 and treated every electrostatic field whose $g_{tt}$ is a function of the electric potential [majumdar1947]. Where $g_{tt}$ is the square of the potential plus a constant, he reduced the field equations to Laplace's equation for a single function, $U$ in $$ds^2 = -\frac{c^2dt^2}{U^2} + U^2\left(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2\right)$$ [majumdar1947]. Achilles Papapetrou found the same solution for an arbitrary distribution of charge in the same year [papapetrou1947].¶In Newton's theory point masses whose charges equal $G^{1/2}$ times their masses stay at rest in any arrangement, since the electric repulsion between every pair cancels their gravitational attraction [hartle1972]. Majumdar and Papapetrou's metric is the relativistic form of that balance: with $U = 1 + \sum_i m_i/|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i|$ it holds any number of such sources at rest at any points [hartle1972, griffiths2009]. Charged dust in static equilibrium, uniformly charged or with equipotential boundaries, must have its charge density equal to its mass density, and its $g_{tt}$ is then a function of the potential, as Utpal Kumar De and Amal Kumar Raychaudhuri showed in 1968 [de1968]. Dust with certain other ratios of charge to mass also has equilibrium configurations, which William Bonnor found in 1980 and which in general contain singularities [bonnor1980dust].¶Each point $\mathbf{x}_i$ is a surface of area $4\pi m_i^2$, a stationary null surface that is the event horizon of an extremal charged black hole, through which the solution "can be analytically extended", as James Hartle and Stephen Hawking showed in 1972 [hartle1972]. Beyond each horizon the extension reaches regions bounded by a curvature singularity [hartle1972]. A single hole is the extremal Reissner-Nordström black hole, and $N$ holes are $N$ of them in equilibrium [griffiths2009, hartle1972]. Spinning sources whose charge equals their mass carry the metric over to stationary fields, built from solutions of Laplace's equation by Zoltán Perjés in 1971 and by Werner Israel and Gordon Wilson in 1972 [perjes1971, israel1972]. Hartle and Hawking found that every asymptotically flat member of that stationary class they examined has a naked singularity, and conjectured that the static Majumdar-Papapetrou black holes are the only stationary Einstein-Maxwell black holes of several components without one [hartle1972].¶Piotr Chruściel and Nikolai Nadirashvili proved in 1995 that every electrovacuum Majumdar-Papapetrou spacetime with a black hole region and a regular domain of outer communications is a standard one, finitely many extremal Reissner-Nordström holes held at rest, with $U = 1 + \sum_i m_i/|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i|$ over a finite set of points and every $m_i > 0$ [chrusciel1995]. A static, asymptotically flat electrovacuum black hole whose horizons are all degenerate has an ADM mass equal to its total charge, as Markus Heusler showed in 1997 [heusler1997]. Chruściel, Harvey Reall, and Paul Tod showed in 2006 that under certain conditions every regular black hole of the stationary class of Israel, Wilson, and Perjés belongs to the Majumdar-Papapetrou family, which settles Hartle and Hawking's conjecture on those conditions [chrusciel2006, griffiths2009]. Chruściel and Tod proved in 2007 that a static electrovacuum black hole cannot mix degenerate and nondegenerate horizons [chrusciel2007].¶With their total mass equal to their total charge, the holes attain the lower bound on the mass of a spacetime in terms of its electric and magnetic charges that Gary Gibbons and Christopher Hull derived in 1982, the analogue of Bogomolny's bound for magnetic monopoles [gibbons1982, heusler1997]. In four dimensions the metric extends analytically through every horizon [hartle1972, welch1995, candlish2007]. In five or more dimensions the curvature stays bounded at a horizon and some of its derivatives diverge there, so the metric is only finitely differentiable, as Dean Welch showed in 1995 [welch1995]. Graeme Candlish and Harvey Reall sharpened that in 2007: in five dimensions the metric of holes on a common axis is generically $C^2$ but not $C^3$ at a horizon, and in more than five it is $C^1$ but not $C^2$, with a curvature singularity in a parallelly propagated frame [candlish2007].¶Robert Ferrell and Douglas Eardley let the holes move slowly in 1987 and calculated their scattering and coalescence exactly in that limit [ferrell1987]. David Kastor and Jennie Traschen found in 1993 analytic solutions for any number of holes of charge equal to mass in a universe with a positive cosmological constant, which reduce to Majumdar and Papapetrou's at $\Lambda = 0$, are "highly dynamical", and merge where the holes approach one another [kastor1993]. The horizon of the merged hole "is not smooth", as Dieter Brill, Gary Horowitz, Kastor, and Traschen found in 1994 [brill1994]. Light moving among two fixed holes is chaotic: George Contopoulos found in 1990 that the initial conditions of its three kinds of orbit "form three Cantor sets" [contopoulos1990]. Two equal holes of mass $M$ hold stable bounded orbits of light for separations between $a_1 = 4M/\sqrt{27}$ and $\sqrt{2}\,a_1$, as Jake Shipley and Sam Dolan found in 2016 when they drew the shadow of the pair [shipley2016].

related.text: A single hole of the family is the extremal Reissner-Nordström black hole in isotropic coordinates [hartle1972, griffiths2009].
The geometry down the throat of each hole. In the limit toward any one of them $U \approx m_i/|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i|$, and the metric is that of AdS$_2 \times$ S$^2$.
Another solution built on $1 + \sum_i m_i/|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i|$: any number of Kaluza-Klein monopoles stay at rest wherever they are put, as these black holes do [hawking1977, ruback1986].
The same holes in a universe with a positive cosmological constant, where they ride the expansion and no longer stand still. Holes that fall together merge [kastor1993, brill1994].

The charged black hole in de Sitter space. With charge equal to mass it is the single hole of David Kastor and Jennie Traschen's solutions of 1993, Majumdar and Papapetrou's holes in a universe with $\Lambda > 0$, where they move and merge [kastor1993].
The same charges set spinning. Israel, Wilson, and Perjés let $U$ be complex, and the black holes among their fields are these static ones [hartle1972, chrusciel2006].
Two black objects of five dimensions held apart with no charge: a ring kept from falling onto the hole at its centre by rotation [elvang2007].

Two spinning black holes on one axis, with no charge. The repulsion between their spins does not balance their attraction, so a strut holds them apart where these holes need none [kramer1980, neugebauer2009].

A space of four dimensions with no time, built on the same sum of potentials $1/|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i|$ over flat space, with two terms and no constant. Its two centres are regular points, the poles of a 2-sphere [gibbonshawking1978, ishihara2006].

One moment of two black holes at rest with any masses and charges, which Dieter Brill and Richard Lindquist found in 1963. Where every charge equals its mass, their slice is a moment of Majumdar and Papapetrou's holes [brill1963].
Two extremal black holes of opposite charge. Gravity and the charges both pull, so a strut on the axis holds the pair apart [emparan2000].

One charge in the same balance, spread on a shell. Arnowitt, Deser, and Misner shrank it to a point in 1960 and found the mass fixed by the charge, with the single hole's field outside [arnowitt1960].
Many bodies with no charge to hold them apart. They orbit, and their field is known to the first order beyond Newton, where Majumdar and Papapetrou's is exact [einstein1938].
